summary: Year 5 pupils (age 9-10) learn to DEDUCE missing lengths and angles of a rectangle from its defining properties (four right angles; two pairs of equal opposite sides) and the given numbers, rather than measuring the diagram. Core work: find a missing side from a given side and the perimeter (P = 2(l+w): halve, then subtract) or from a given side and the area (A = l×w: divide); state that the fourth angle must be 90°; attach correct units (cm, cm²). The deliberately not-to-scale drawing forces reliance on numbers and properties. The dominant obstacle is confusing area with perimeter (and their inverse operations); others are reading lengths/angles off an inaccurate picture, short-cutting the perimeter inverse (subtracting from the whole perimeter instead of from half), and forgetting that one given side already fixes its opposite.
misconceptions: Confuses area and perimeter, or their formulae/units — e.g. divides by a side when the problem gave the perimeter, or halves the area (Machaba: taught together, learned instrumentally)
Short-cuts the perimeter inverse — subtracts the known side straight from the whole perimeter instead of from half of it
Reads unknown lengths or angles off the not-to-scale diagram instead of deducing them from the properties and givens
Forgets that opposite sides are equal, so treats all four sides as unknown even after one is given, or doubts that the fourth angle is 90°

activities.title: Deduce the missing side: perimeter then area, from a not-to-scale rectangle
steps: Work with a rectangle labelled '8 cm' on one side and 'perimeter = 28 cm', drawn deliberately almost square so measuring is useless; one side is a blank box.
Before calculating, mark the equal opposite sides (tick marks) and the four squared (90°) corners so the given 8 cm is seen on its opposite side too.
Reason the perimeter case aloud or in writing: two sides are 8; the four sides total 28; half the perimeter is 14; 14 - 8 = 6, so the missing side is 6 cm.
Switch to an area task: '48 cm², one side 8 cm' — divide 48 ÷ 8 = 6 to find the missing side, and note the inside is filled by a 6-by-8 region.
State the size of the fourth angle (90°) and justify it from the definition, not the picture.
Attach units throughout: cm for sides, cm² for area.
Transfer to a fresh rectangle with different numbers, choosing halve-then-subtract for perimeter and divide for area.
activities.insight: Missing facts about a rectangle are deduced from its properties and the given numbers, not read off the drawing; 'going round' (perimeter: halve, then subtract) and 'filling in' (area: divide) are different inverse operations that must be chosen by what the problem gives.

activities.title: Short-answer deductions with targeted wrong-answer options
steps: Given one side and the perimeter, construct the other side (e.g. side 8 cm, perimeter 28 cm → fill in 6 cm) and show the halve-then-subtract working.
Given the area and one side, find the other side (e.g. 48 cm², one side 8 cm → 6 cm) and show the division.
Answer a units item: decide whether a given answer should be in cm or cm².
Face a not-to-scale figure whose proportions mislead, and justify the answer from the numbers rather than the look.
When choosing among options, reject the halved-area answer and the subtract-from-whole-perimeter answer (28 - 8 = 20) and explain why each is wrong.
activities.insight: The child can reliably select and carry out the correct inverse operation and attach the correct unit, resisting the area/perimeter confusion and the not-to-scale picture.

activities.title: Rectangle properties reference card
steps: Consult a labelled rectangle: each corner reveals '90°', each side reveals 'equals its opposite', and the formulae P = 2(l+w) and A = l×w reveal their undo steps.
Use it alongside practice to recall the defining properties before calculating.

Answer NCETM-style reasoning probes: 'Tell me some facts about rectangles'; 'Is it possible for a rectangle to have only three right angles?'; 'What is the same and what is different about a square and a rectangle?'
activities.insight: A rectangle's defining properties — two pairs of equal opposite sides and four right angles — are the authority for deduction, and holding them in mind prevents treating sides or the fourth angle as unknown.

checkQuestion: Give the child a rectangle drawn deliberately NOT to scale (make it look almost square), with one side labelled 8 cm, the perimeter labelled 28 cm, and one side left blank — plus a second rectangle with area 48 cm² and one side 8 cm. Say: 'Find the missing side of each, and tell me the size of the fourth angle. Show your working.' Say nothing about method; watch how they get the missing sides and whether they measure the picture or reason from the numbers.
checkAnswer: First rectangle: reasons that opposite sides are equal, so half the perimeter is 14 cm and the missing side = 14 - 8 = 6 cm; states that all angles, including the fourth, are 90°. Second rectangle: missing side = 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm. Uses the given numbers and rectangle properties (not the drawing), with correct units (cm and cm²).
